 Binance Calls 335.9M-Line Leak Claim Likely Scam [2026]
 Ryan Cole 
 Updated Nov 9, 2026 · 17 min read 
 Binance moved fast to knock down a headline that had been spreading across an underground forum and X. The exchange said a claim attributed to ShinyHunters, which alleged the theft of 335,900,000 lines of information, was likely a scam and not evidence of a breach of Binance systems. Crypto News, The Cryptonomist, Newsbytes.PH, Dataconomy and CyberInsider all carried the story.

 The denial is preliminary, and Binance said it is still investigating. Still, the exchange told reporters its early review found no evidence that customer identity-verification data, account credentials, wallet private keys or internal infrastructure information had been compromised in connection with the listing. For anyone tracking exchange security, this follows other crypto-security stories we have covered, including Elliptic’s tracing of funds tied to a Binance hack . This one differs because Binance says nothing was stolen at all.
 This analysis separates what the sources actually report from what the seller merely asserts. It also explains why a big number in a forum post does not equal a big number of victims, and what users should do while the review runs. Every figure below comes from the named outlets or from ThreatMon’s reporting as relayed by them. Anything we could not confirm is labeled that way.

 Add now Binance Says the 335.9M-Line Claim Looks Like a Scam
 The core facts fit in a few sentences. A listing credited to ShinyHunters claimed to hold 335,900,000 lines of information tied to Binance. Binance reviewed the description and the sample data it was shown, then said the offer appears likely to be a scam rather than proof that its systems were breached. The company also said it is investigating.
 A Binance spokesperson put it this way: “Based on the description provided and the sample information reviewed so far, this appears likely to be a scam rather than evidence of a Binance systems breach.” That sentence is carefully hedged. It says “likely” and “appears,” and it ties the conclusion to the sample information reviewed so far. It does not say the listing is proven fake, and it does not close the investigation.

 That hedging matters for readers who want a clean yes or no. The responsible reading is that Binance has found no sign of compromise in its early review, while independent confirmation is still missing on both sides. Nobody outside Binance has published a forensic analysis of the sample, and the seller has not, per the reports we reviewed, offered proof that survives scrutiny.
 Search interest in the story is high because the number is dramatic. A figure above 335 million sounds like it would cover most of any exchange’s user base, which is exactly why the claim travels. Yet the sourcing is thin, and the central number has not been confirmed as a count of people.
 What the Listing Alleges, in Plain Terms
 According to the outlets covering the story, the advertised dataset was described as including email addresses, telephone numbers, passwords, identification documents and transaction histories. That is a long list of sensitive material, and a seller who wants a high price has every incentive to claim all of it. ThreatMon reported that the advertised data allegedly covered users in roughly 170 countries.
 Two further claims drew attention. Some versions of the listing suggested the data included KYC documents, hot-wallet asset information or wallet private keys. Binance’s preliminary review found no evidence of that, and none of the outlets reported independent proof. We treat those items as unconfirmed.
 The claim reportedly circulated on an underground forum and on X. That combination is common. A forum post establishes the offer for would-be buyers, while a post on X pushes the claim to journalists, traders and the exchange’s own customers. The second audience is often the real target, because public pressure can matter more to a scammer than a single sale.
 Claim Versus Response: A Status Table
 The table below lays out each element of the story, who reported it, and where it stands today. It uses only details from the reporting by the named outlets and ThreatMon.
 Element What was reported Status on Nov. 9, 2026 
 Size of claimed theft 335,900,000 lines of information Unconfirmed 
 Attribution Claim attributed to ShinyHunters Attribution is part of the claim, not verified 
 Binance verdict Likely a scam, not a systems breach Preliminary, investigation continues 
 Reach of dataset About 170 countries (ThreatMon) Seller’s claim 
 Asking price $900,000 in Bitcoin or Monero (ThreatMon) Seller’s demand 
 Data types listed Emails, phone numbers, passwords, ID documents, transaction histories Unconfirmed as genuine Binance data 
 KYC, hot-wallet, private keys Alleged in some descriptions Unconfirmed, Binance found no evidence 
 335 million affected users Line count read as people Unconfirmed, lines are not people 
 Where it spread Underground forum and X Reported 
 Every row marked unconfirmed is a place where a headline can run ahead of the facts. The only element Binance has addressed directly is the verdict, and even that carries the word “preliminary.”
 Why 335,900,000 Lines Does Not Mean 335 Million Users
 The most misleading shortcut in this story is the leap from “lines” to “users.” A line in a database dump is a row of text. One customer can generate dozens of rows across email records, login events, device records, deposits, withdrawals and trades. A dataset with 335,900,000 lines could describe far fewer people than the raw number suggests, and a dataset padded with duplicates or fabricated rows could describe almost nobody.
 Reporting on the claim noted the same gap. The advertised line count was not confirmed as a number of people, so any headline saying 335 million users were affected goes beyond the evidence. We avoid that phrasing here for the same reason.
 The padding problem
 Scam listings often inflate size because size sells. Sellers can combine old, public or recycled data from unrelated sources, repeat rows, or generate plausible-looking records. A buyer who cannot inspect the full file has to trust the seller’s description. That asymmetry is the whole business model of a fake listing.
 Why a sample proves little
 Sellers usually release a small sample to prove authenticity. Binance said it reviewed sample information, and its conclusion was that the offer looks like a scam. A sample can fail in several ways. The records might not match any real account, the formats might not match Binance’s systems, or the data might trace to older, unrelated exposures. Binance did not publish its detailed reasoning, so outsiders cannot yet check which of those applied.
 ThreatMon’s Details: 170 Countries and a $900,000 Price
 ThreatMon, a threat-intelligence firm, supplied the most specific details in the coverage. It reported that the seller demanded $900,000, payable in Bitcoin or Monero, and that the dataset allegedly spanned users in about 170 countries. Those two points shaped how the story was framed, so they deserve a closer look.
 Start with the price. Asking $900,000 for 335.9 million lines works out to about a quarter of a cent per line. If the data were authentic and complete, it would carry far more value on the criminal market for fraud, account takeover and phishing. That arithmetic does not prove the listing is fake, but it fits the pattern Binance described. A seller with real, fresh exchange data would have little reason to price it so low.
 Next, the payment method. Bitcoin and Monero are the usual currencies on underground markets, and Monero in particular is chosen for its privacy features. The payment terms tell us how the seller wants to get paid. They tell us nothing about whether the data is real.
 Finally, the 170-country figure. Binance serves a global audience, so a claim of worldwide coverage sounds plausible. Plausibility is cheap, though. A fabricated dataset can list any set of countries it likes. ThreatMon reported what the listing claimed. The outlets did not present it as a verified finding.
 How Binance Reached Its Preliminary Conclusion
 Binance’s public statement points to two inputs: the description of the dataset and the sample information reviewed so far. It then reports an absence of evidence across five areas. The company said it found no sign that its systems, customer identity-verification data, account credentials, wallet private keys or internal infrastructure information had been compromised in connection with the listing.
 An absence of evidence is not an absence of risk, and security professionals know the difference. A preliminary review can miss things, particularly if an attacker compromised a third-party vendor rather than the exchange itself. Binance did not claim otherwise. It said it is investigating, which keeps the door open for an update.
 What the statement does rule out, for now, is the most alarming reading, in which attackers took KYC files, hot-wallet information or private keys straight from Binance infrastructure. Private keys in particular would be a catastrophic exposure for any exchange. Binance said it saw no evidence of that, and the independent coverage reported no proof either.
 Readers who want to see how external researchers handle disputed vulnerability and exposure claims can look at our overview of bug bounty platforms , where triage teams verify submissions before anyone treats them as real.
 Why a Scam Listing Can Still Cause Harm
 Calling something a scam does not make it harmless. A fake breach listing can hurt users and the exchange in several concrete ways, even when no Binance data was taken.
 Panic withdrawals. Customers who believe the headline may pull funds or close accounts, which can strain support teams and distort short-term flows.
 Phishing opportunities. Criminals often piggyback on a breach rumor. Emails and texts claiming to help “secure your account” can arrive within hours.
 Buyer fraud. Anyone who pays the seller risks losing the money and receiving worthless or recycled data. Binance’s verdict suggests that outcome is likely.
 Reputation damage. Even a debunked claim leaves search results and social posts that repeat the 335 million figure for months.
 The second item deserves the most attention from ordinary users. During any exchange-related scare, scammers know that people are anxious and checking their inboxes. A message that appears to come from Binance and asks you to click a link, confirm a password or share an identity document is the real danger here, whatever happened to the forum listing.

 Our earlier report on DigiCert’s confirmed breach of identity-document archives shows why identity documents are such a prized target. If real ID scans leak anywhere, they cannot be reset like a password, so the stakes of a false alarm and a true alarm both stay high.
 Historical Context: Data-for-Sale Listings and Company Denials
 Underground forums have hosted data-for-sale listings for years, and the cycle is familiar. A seller posts a dramatic claim against a well-known brand. Researchers and journalists amplify it. The company reviews the sample and either confirms a breach or says the data is old, scraped or fake. Over time, the pattern has taught analysts to treat the first day or two of any listing with caution.
 Three outcomes recur. In the first, the company confirms an incident, publishes details and notifies affected people. In the second, the data turns out to come from an older or third-party source, so it is real but not new. In the third, the listing is fabricated or padded, which is the outcome Binance is signaling here. Which category a given listing falls into usually becomes clear only after outside researchers examine the sample.
 Crypto exchanges carry extra exposure to this cycle. They hold identity documents, financial histories and assets, so a believable claim gets attention quickly. Their customers also tend to follow security news closely and share it on X, which speeds the spread of unverified numbers. Binance’s response came at the speed the medium demands, with a spokesperson statement, a specific verdict and a commitment to keep investigating.
 We should add one caution. A company statement is a data point, not the last word. Early company messaging can be revised as an investigation matures. The right posture is to watch for the next update from Binance and any independent analysis of the sample.
 Market Impact: What Moves and What Does Not
 None of the outlets we reviewed reported a measured price reaction tied to this claim, so we will not invent one. What we can describe is the channel through which a false breach story would reach markets, and the reasons this one may have limited reach.
 Exchange breach fears usually hit sentiment first. Traders worry about custody, withdrawals and counterparty risk. A fast denial that names the data categories at issue, as Binance’s did, helps cap that worry. The company’s statement targeted the highest-risk items directly, namely private keys, credentials and identity-verification data.
 Broader crypto sentiment is already fragile, as our coverage of the post-midterm crypto slide showed. In a weak tape, security scares can carry more weight than they would in a calm one. That said, no source attributes any specific move to this listing, and we make no such claim.
 Insurers and counterparties watch these episodes too. Our report on insurer scrutiny of crypto firms covers how underwriters look at security claims. A debunked listing should not change underwriting by itself, but it adds to the paper trail those teams read when they assess how an exchange handles disclosure.
 Confirmed Breach Versus Unverified Listing: A Comparison
 Readers often ask how to tell the two situations apart in real time. The table below compares the signals that usually accompany each. It describes general patterns, and it applies them to the facts reported so far on the Binance claim.
 Signal Typical confirmed breach Typical unverified listing Binance claim today 
 Who first announces it The affected company The seller or a forum poster Seller, via forum and X 
 Company statement Acknowledges an incident and scope Denies or disputes the claim Says likely a scam 
 Description of data Named categories with timing Broad list, large headline number Broad list, 335,900,000 lines 
 Unit of measure People or accounts affected Lines, rows or records Lines, not confirmed as people 
 Independent verification Researchers match samples to real accounts Samples fail to match or look recycled No public verification yet 
 User guidance Password resets and notices General caution against phishing Caution is prudent 
 For a case where a company did confirm an incident and named specific data types, compare the Gnosis Pay breach report . Confirmed incidents tend to describe what was taken in concrete terms. The Binance listing instead leans on a large round claim and a long list of the most alarming data categories.
 What Verification Would Look Like
 Moving this story from “likely a scam” to “settled” needs evidence that outsiders can examine. Several kinds of evidence would do it, and the lack of them today is part of why the claim stays unconfirmed.
 Evidence that would support the seller
 A seller with genuine data could show records that map to real, verifiable accounts, with details that only an insider system would hold. Independent researchers could then confirm the match without exposing the underlying people. Nothing in the coverage so far indicates that happened. Binance, for its part, said its review of the sample found no evidence of compromise.
 Evidence that would settle it for Binance
 Binance could strengthen its case by publishing a fuller technical explanation, such as why the sample records do not match its systems, or by sharing findings with reputable outside analysts. The company has not done so yet, according to the reporting we reviewed. A completed investigation with a clear statement would carry more weight than a preliminary one.

 Security teams checking their own exposure to this kind of claim can use the practices in our guide to vulnerability scanning tools for lean teams . Scanners cannot disprove a forum claim, but they help organizations confirm their own external attack surface before they respond.
 What Binance Users Should Do Now
 Binance’s preliminary finding is reassuring, but sensible habits cost almost nothing. Users do not need to panic. They should tighten a few settings and stay alert for follow-on scams.
 Check your login security. Use a unique password for your exchange account and turn on app-based two-factor authentication.
 Review withdrawal protections. Enable any available address allowlisting and anti-phishing codes in your account settings.
 Distrust unsolicited messages. Do not click links in emails or texts that mention a breach. Open the official app or type the address yourself.
 Never share ID documents on request. A legitimate exchange will not ask you to send identity scans through a chat message or a form from an unknown link.
 Watch for official updates. Binance said it is investigating, so a follow-up is possible. Rely on the company’s own channels for it.
 Users who reuse a password across several sites should change it regardless of this story. Password reuse remains one of the most common ways a leak at one service turns into a compromise at another.
 Five Predictions for the Next Few Weeks
 These are our own readings of the situation, drawn from the pattern of past cases. They are judgments, not facts, and none comes from Binance or any named expert.
 Binance will likely publish a follow-up. The company said it is investigating, and a closing statement is the natural next step once its review finishes.
 Independent analysts will probably weigh in on the sample. If the sample circulates, outside researchers can check whether records match real accounts or older, unrelated data.
 Phishing tied to the story is a real risk. Scam emails that borrow the breach headline tend to appear quickly, and users should expect some.
 Misreadings of “335 million” will persist. Some outlets and social posts will keep treating lines as users, even though that reading is unconfirmed.
 Exchanges will tighten how they answer listings. A fast, specific denial like this one is becoming a template, and rivals watching it will likely copy the approach.
 For broader context on how breach stories and exchange security are shaping the industry, see our security coverage hub .
 What Remains Unconfirmed
 Because the story is moving, a short ledger of open points helps. We list them here so readers can tell facts from assertions when they see the story repeated elsewhere.
 The alleged theft of 335,900,000 lines of user data is unconfirmed.
 The idea that the data includes KYC documents, hot-wallet asset information or wallet private keys is unconfirmed.
 The reading of 335,900,000 lines as 335 million affected users is unconfirmed, since the line count was not confirmed as a number of people.
 Any actual Binance data breach or exposure of customer information is unconfirmed.
 Confirmed, by contrast, is a short list. Binance publicly called the claim likely a scam. Binance said its preliminary review found no evidence of compromise across its systems, identity-verification data, credentials, private keys and internal infrastructure. And ThreatMon reported the roughly 170-country scope and the $900,000 demand in Bitcoin or Monero. Beyond that, readers should treat each new detail as unverified until a named source confirms it.
 The Takeaway for Readers and Security Teams
 This episode shows how a single forum post can generate a global news cycle with no confirmed breach behind it. Binance’s response was quick, specific and appropriately hedged. The facts available today support caution toward the seller’s claims, and equal caution toward anyone declaring the matter closed.
 For security teams, the lesson is to prepare a response template before a claim lands. Name the data categories at issue, say what the review has found, commit to updates and warn users about opportunistic phishing. For readers, the lesson is simpler. Ask what a big number actually measures, who is reporting it, and whether anyone independent has checked it.
 We will update this analysis if Binance completes its investigation or if independent researchers publish findings on the sample.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Did Binance confirm a data breach?
 No. Binance said the claim attributed to ShinyHunters was likely a scam and not evidence of a breach of its systems. Its preliminary review found no evidence that its systems, customer identity-verification data, account credentials, wallet private keys or internal infrastructure information had been compromised in connection with the listing.
 How many Binance users were affected?
 There is no confirmed number. The listing advertised 335,900,000 lines of information, but that line count was not confirmed as a number of people. Reading it as 335 million affected users goes beyond the evidence, and Binance says it found no breach.
 What did the seller reportedly ask for?
 ThreatMon reported that the seller demanded $900,000, payable in Bitcoin or Monero. ThreatMon also reported that the advertised dataset allegedly covered users in about 170 countries. Both points are the seller’s claims, not verified facts.
 What data did the listing claim to include?
 The dataset was described as including email addresses, telephone numbers, passwords, identification documents and transaction histories. Claims that it also held KYC documents, hot-wallet asset information or wallet private keys remain unconfirmed, and Binance found no evidence of those.
 Is the investigation finished?
 No. Binance described its conclusion as preliminary and said it is investigating. A final statement could change the picture, so users should watch Binance’s official channels for updates.
 Should I change my Binance password?
 Binance reported no evidence that credentials were compromised, so there is no confirmed reason to reset. Still, using a unique password and app-based two-factor authentication is good practice, and it costs little. If you reuse your password on other sites, change it.
 Which outlets reported the story?
 Crypto News, The Cryptonomist, Newsbytes.PH, Dataconomy and CyberInsider covered the claim and Binance’s response, with ThreatMon supplying details on the alleged dataset and the seller’s demand.
 How can I avoid scams tied to this story?
 Ignore unsolicited emails, texts and direct messages that mention a breach and ask you to click a link or share documents. Open the official Binance app or type the address yourself, and never send identity documents through an unverified channel.
